title: Likelihood as a function of the parameter
dek: Freeze the data, unfreeze θ. L(θ | y) = f(y | θ) is not a density in θ. Profile, relative, and score are how you read that curve.
story: The sampling model f(y | θ) becomes a likelihood when y is treated as fixed. Nothing in that sentence gives you a probability distribution on θ. Integrating L with respect to θ without a prior is a category error; maximising it is not.

Working on ℓ(θ) = log L is numerical hygiene: products of small densities become sums. The score S(θ) = ∇ℓ is the gradient. Interior MLEs solve S(θ̂) = 0. Observed information −∇²ℓ(θ̂) is the local curvature of the same curve.

When θ = (ψ, λ) and ψ is the scientific target, the profile likelihood L_p(ψ) = max_λ L(ψ, λ) is the honest 1-D slice. A Wald interval from a transformation you have not profiled can look prettier than the likelihood and be wrong near a boundary — allele frequencies, variance components, mixture weights.
deep: Relative likelihood R(θ) = L(θ)/L(θ̂). Contours R ≥ 0.15 are a classical sketch of “plausible θ” without converting the curve into a posterior. They are not confidence sets until you add a sampling argument (Wilks, Bartlett, simulation).

Score identity: under regularity, E_θ[S(θ)] = 0 and Var(S) = I(θ) = E[−∇²ℓ]. The MLE is the root of a mean-zero estimating equation. Sandwich covariance appears when that identity fails because f was misspecified.

Profile likelihood ratio 2(ℓ(θ̂) − ℓ_p(ψ)) is the LRT for H₀: ψ = ψ₀ with nuisance λ fitted under the restriction. This is the same object as Wilks on a nested pair. Do not profile by plugging in a consistent λ̂ from the full model and calling it a profile — that is a Wald-flavoured shortcut.

In a sequencing lab, the likelihood is often a product over sites or isolates only after you have declared independence. A phylogenetic likelihood replaces that product with a tree-indexed Markov process. The word “likelihood” did not change; the joint f(y | θ) did.

formulas.label: Likelihood and log-likelihood
formulas.expression: L(θ | y) = f(y | θ),   ℓ(θ) = log L(θ | y)
formulas.note: L is not a density in θ. ℓ is a numerically stabler coordinate.

formulas.label: Profile likelihood
formulas.note: Maximise nuisance parameters at each fixed scientific target ψ.

visual.caption: Schematic readings of one experiment: a peaked likelihood after a large n, a flatter likelihood after a small n, and a skewed profile that is not a Normal sampling law. The x-axis is θ, not y.

example.title: Profile a transmission probability on the logit scale
example.setup: n = 40 independent household contacts, Yᵢ ~ Bernoulli(π), π = logit⁻¹(ψ). You care about π, but the curvature is more regular in ψ. Data: y = 6 positives.

steps.title: Write L
steps.body: L(π) = π⁶ (1−π)³⁴ on (0,1). Equivalently ℓ(ψ) = 6ψ − 40 log(1+e^ψ) with π = e^ψ/(1+e^ψ).

steps.title: Maximise
steps.body: Score 6 − 40π = 0 ⇒ π̂ = 6/40 = 0.15, ψ̂ = logit(0.15). Relative likelihood R(π) = L(π)/L(0.15) can be plotted on π directly.

steps.title: Why profile language still matters
steps.body: If a second parameter (household random intercept) is present, π is no longer a one-dimensional exponential-family mean. You must maximise the nuisance at each π, not freeze the random-effect variance at its full-model MLE and call the slice a profile.

example.takeaway: Draw L as a function of the scientific parameter. If nuisances exist, maximise them; do not condition on a plugged-in favourite.

choices: Always, because likelihoods are densities in θ
Only after you multiply by a prior and normalise, i.e. once you have a posterior
Whenever the model is an exponential family
check.answer: Only after you multiply by a prior and normalise, i.e. once you have a posterior
check.why: L(· | y) is a function of θ, not a probability density, unless you add p(θ) and divide by the marginal.

whyWrong.Whenever the model is an exponential fam: Exponential families still need a prior to make a posterior.
whyWrong.When n > 30: Sample size does not normalise L.

check.prompt: Bernoulli n = 10, y = 3. Score S(π) = 3/π − 7/(1−π). At π = 0.3 the score is:
check.why: π̂ = y/n = 0.3 is the MLE, so the interior score is zero there: 3/0.3 − 7/0.7 = 10 − 10 = 0.

whyWrong.1: The score is a derivative, not a probability.
whyWrong.10: That is 3/0.3 before subtracting the second term.

check.prompt: On the likelihood plate the x-axis is labelled as a parameter. What mistake does that figure refuse?
check.figureHint: Three curves of L(θ | y) on θ.
choices: Treating the likelihood curve as a sampling density of Y
Using a log scale for ℓ
check.answer: Treating the likelihood curve as a sampling density of Y
check.why: The whole point of the plate is that after y is observed the remaining free coordinate is θ. Those curves are not densities of the data.

whyWrong.Profiling a nuisance parameter: That is how you read a multi-parameter L.
whyWrong.Reporting an MLE: The peak of L is the MLE.
